The '''2017–18 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team''' represented [[Georgetown University]] in the [[2017–18 NCAA Division I men's basketball season]]. The Hoyas, led by first-year head coach [[Patrick Ewing]], played their home games at the [[Capital One Arena]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] as members of the [[Big East Conference]]. They finished the season 15–15, 5–13 in Big East play to finish in eighth place. They lost in the first round of the [[2018 Big East men's basketball tournament|Big East tournament]] to [[2017–18 St. John's Red Storm men's basketball team|St. John's]].

==Previous season==
The [[2016–17 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|Hoyas]] finished the [[2016–17 NCAA Division I men's basketball season|2016–17 season]] at 14–18, 5–13 in [[2016–17 Big East Conference men's basketball season|Big East play]], to finish in ninth place in the conference. As the No. 9 seed in the [[2017 Big East men's basketball tournament|Big East tournament]], they lost in the first round to [[2016–17 St. John's Red Storm men's basketball team|St. John's]]. Georgetown finished the season with a losing record for the second straight year, the first time that had happened since the [[1971–72 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1971–72]] and [[1972–73 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1972–73]] seasons, and without an invitation to a postseason tournament in consecutive years for the first time since 1973 and 1974.

On March 23, 2017, Georgetown officials announced that head coach [[John Thompson III]] had been [[dismissal (employment)|fired]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/story/_/id/18984268/georgetown-hoyas-parting-ways-john-thompson-iii|title=Hoyas dismiss coach John Thompson III after 13 seasons|publisher=[[ESPN]]|author=Jeff Goodman and Jeff Borzello|date=2017-03-23|access-date=2017-03-23}}</ref><ref>[http://www.thehoya.com/john-thompson-iii-fired-after-two-consecutive-losing-seasons/ Santamaria, Paolo B., and Sean Hoffman, "John Thompson III Fired After 2 Consecutive Losing Seasons," thehoya.com, March 23, 2017.]</ref><ref>[https://www.si.com/college-basketball/2017/03/23/ Anonymous, "Georgetown fires head coach John Thompson III after 13 years," si.com, March 23, 2017.]{{Dead link|date=September 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> On April 2, it was reported that [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|Basketball Hall of Famer]] and Georgetown alumnus Patrick Ewing would replace Thompson as head coach.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/ncaab/bigeast/2017/04/03/patrick-ewing-georgetown-coach/99988542/|title=Patrick Ewing hired as coach of Georgetown|work=USA TODAY|access-date=2017-04-03|language=en}}</ref>

==Arrival of Patrick Ewing==
[[File:Ewing on court.jpg|left|thumb|Head coach [[Patrick Ewing]] on court in April 2018]]On April 3, 2017, Georgetown hired [[Patrick Ewing]] to replace the fired [[John Thompson III]] as head coach. Generally considered the greatest player in Georgetown men's basketball history, Ewing had led the Georgetown teams of [[1981–82 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1981]] through [[1984–85 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1985]], which had reached the [[NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament]]′s championship game three times and won one national championship, in [[1984 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1984]]. He then went on to a [[Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame]] 17-season playing career in the [[National Basketball Association]], playing for the [[New York Knicks]] from [[1985–86 New York Knicks season|1985]] to [[1999–2000 New York Knicks season|2000]], the [[Seattle SuperSonics]] from [[2000–01 Seattle SuperSonics season|2000 to 2001]], and the [[Orlando Magic]] from [[2001–02 Orlando Magic season|2001 to 2002]]. After that, he spent 15 years as an NBA assistant coach, with the [[Washington Wizards]] from [[2002–03 Washington Wizards season|2002 to 2003]], the [[Houston Rockets]] from [[2003–04 Houston Rockets season|2003]] to [[2005–06 Houston Rockets season|2006]], the Orlando Magic from [[2007–08 Orlando Magic season|2007]] to [[2011–12 Orlando Magic season|2012]], and the [[Charlotte Hornets|Charlotte Bobcats/Charlotte Hornets]] from [[2012–13 Charlotte Bobcats season|2012]] to [[2016–17 Charlotte Hornets season|2017]]. Although he had made it clear that he desired a head coaching job in the NBA and had interviewed for head coaching positions, he had never been a head coach at any level before taking the job at Georgetown. After taking over at Georgetown, he told the press that he never would have considered taking a college coaching job anywhere except at Georgetown where, he said, "I was able to...spend four of the best years of my life."<ref name=wallace20171108>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/as-georgetown-basketball-coach-patrick-ewing-has-been-forced-into-a-higher-tempo/2017/11/08/5f89038c-c48e-11e7-84bc-5e285c7f4512_story.html Wallace, Ava, "As Georgetown basketball coach, Patrick Ewing has been forced into a higher tempo," washingtonpost.com, November 8, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref>

After graduating from Georgetown in 1985, Ewing had left the world of college basketball behind completely during his 32 years of playing and coaching in the NBA.<ref name=wallace20171108/> The role of a college coach differed significantly from that of an NBA coach: Player acquisition was very different, requiring compliance with a myriad of [[National Collegiate Athletic Association]] recruiting and eligibility rules and a nearly constant recruiting effort.<ref name=wallace20171108/> Since his college days, much had changed in college basketball, including the rise of the influence of the [[Amateur Athletic Union]] and the orientation of recruiting and coaching toward developing players for NBA careers, as well as the impatience of many college players, who tended to view their college careers as a necessary step on their way to an NBA career but no longer viewed college as a four-year – or even any more than a one-year – commitment. College coaching also required a significant amount of off-court player management, such as ensuring players went to class and met Georgetown's academic eligibility requirements.<ref name=wallace20171108/> Critics of Georgetown's decision to hire Ewing argued that his lack of experience in these matters would undermine his ability to lead the Georgetown program.<ref name=wallace20171108/> Ewing countered that he had a great deal of experience with young NBA players who had foregone some or all of their college eligibility to play in the NBA and that he had hired a staff including assistant coaches [[Louis Orr]] and Robert Kirby – that could provide him with well-informed advice and guide him through the modern world of college basketball. However, his arrival required the departure of his son, [[Patrick Ewing Jr.]], a former Georgetown player who had served under John Thompson III as an assistant coach since August 2015; under Georgetown University's [[nepotism]] policies, the younger Ewing was not allowed to serve in a position in which he reported directly to his father.<ref name=kaduk20170405>[https://sports.yahoo.com/news/patrick-ewings-son-wont-georgetown-staff-nepotism-clause-160455790.html Kaduk, Kevin, "Patrick Ewing's son won't be on Georgetown staff because of 'nepotism clause," yahoo.com, April 5, 2017, 12:04 p.m. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> Many commentators mocked the idea of a nepotism clause at Georgetown given John Thompson III's 13-year tenure as head coach while his father, former Georgetown head coach [[John Thompson (basketball)|John Thompson Jr.]], remained a major figure in the men's basketball program, but the clause did not apply in that case because the younger Thompson was not on his father's staff,<ref name=kaduk20170405/> reporting to athletic director Lee Reed and not to his father.

Ewing said he would abandon John Thompson III's deliberate "[[Princeton offense]]" and move Georgetown's game toward an uptempo, NBA-style offense favored by NBA scouts and more suitable to the playing style of contemporary players.<ref name=wallace20171108/> He also promised a more physical defense of the type that both Georgetown and the [[Big East Conference (1979–2013)|original Big East Conference]] had been known for in their 1980s heyday.<ref name=wallace20171108/> He also told reporters that he thought he could improve Georgetown's recruiting efforts by offering players an easier path to the NBA, which he believed he understood better than most college coaches.<ref name=wallace20171108/>

===Nonconference schedule===

During the head-coaching tenures of [[John Thompson (basketball)|John Thompson Jr.]] and [[Craig Esherick]] in the original Big East Conference between [[1979–80 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1979]] and [[2003–04 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2004]], Georgetown developed a reputation for scheduling weak non-conference opponents, but during his 13 seasons as head coach at Georgetown between [[2004–05 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2004]] and [[2016–17 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2017]], John Thompson III had sought early challenges for his teams during the non-conference portion of the schedule, scheduling ranked opponents, early-season tournaments featuring nationally prominent teams, and distant travel so that his teams could prepare for the Big East Conference season by gaining experience against challenging opponents while facing a demanding travel schedule. Ewing scrapped John Thompson III's approach, returning to the earlier philosophy of arranging a weak early-season schedule. On August 2, in accordance with Ewing's wishes, Georgetown withdrew from the [[Phil Knight Invitational|PK-80–Phil Knight Invitational]], a high-profile, 16-team, two-bracket tournament in [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]], [[Oregon]], scheduled for November 23–26, in which the Hoyas would have opened with a game against [[2017–18 Michigan State Spartans men's basketball team|Michigan State]], a preseason Top Five team, then faced either [[2017–18 Connecticut Huskies men's basketball team|Connecticut]] or [[2017 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2017 Final Four]] participant [[2017–18 Oregon Ducks men's basketball team|Oregon]] in the second round the following day,<ref name=norlander20170802>[https://www.cbssports.com/college-basketball/news/georgetown-wont-be-participating-in-nikes-big-pk80-tournament-in-november-after-all/ Norlander, Matt, "Georgetown won't be participating in Nike's big PK80 tournament in November after all," cbssports.com, August 2, 2017. Retrieved July 24, 2018]</ref> and finished two days later with a final game against [[2017–18 Arkansas Razorbacks men's basketball team|Arkansas]], [[2017–18 North Carolina Tar Heels men's basketball team|North Carolina]], or [[2017–18 Portland Pilots men's basketball team|Portland]]. Big East rival [[2017–18 DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball team|DePaul]] replaced Georgetown in the tournament.<ref name=norlander20170802/> Georgetown athletic director Lee Reed issued a statement explaining the withdrawal, saying "The Georgetown's men's basketball program is in the midst of an exciting time of rebuilding. Georgetown has a prominent, seasoned head coach who has begun this process, which will continue to develop in the fall."<ref name=norlander20170802/> The withdrawal reportedly left Georgetown with nine or ten open slots left to fill in its 2017-2018 schedule, which CBS Sports′ Matt Norlander described on August 2 as "an enormous amount of open dates for a Big East program to fill this deep into the offseason."<ref name=norlander20170802/> But Ewing saw no need to pit his team against some of the toughest teams in the [[United States]] during his first season as head coach, explaining his decision to withdraw this way: "“It's my belief that, why go out there and get my ass kicked to show my recruits that we need their help when I can stay home and watch other people get their butts kicked...Do my recruiting, keep on telling the people we need that we need them, recruit them, and do my job to help my team, build them up and show them what my visions are of them, and win as many games as we can.”<ref name=wallace20170912>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/sports/wp/2017/09/12/georgetowns-first-basketball-schedule-under-patrick-ewing-takes-cues-from-john-thompson/ Wallace, Ava, "Georgetown's first basketball schedule under Patrick Ewing takes cues from John Thompson Jr.," washingtonpost.com, September 12, 2017. Retrieved July 28, 2018]</ref> was the only team among Georgetown's 11 non-conference opponents that made the tournament and did so via an automatic bid by winning the [[2017 Northeast Conference men's basketball tournament|2017 Northeast Conference tournament]] – and none of them were projected to make the [[2018 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|2018 NCAA tournament]];<ref name=miller20170928/> preseason prognosticators raised the possibility that none of them would make even the [[2018 National Invitation Tournament]].<ref name=miller20170928/> Other than a visit to Richmond, the entire non-conference schedule was at home.<ref name=miller20170928/>

Pundits indulged in a chorus of criticism of Georgetown's nonconference schedule. Kerry Miller of [[Bleacher Report]] called the schedule "terrible,"<ref name=miller20170928/> observing that "constructing a strong nonconference schedule for college basketball is an art form, and Georgetown is No. 1 on the list of teams that miserably failed that art class this year"<ref name=miller20170928/> and that "this might be the worst nonconference schedule in major-conference history;"<ref name=miller20170928/> Miller offered the possibility that the Hoyas "could be headed for an interesting dichotomy: Georgetown going 11-0 in nonconference play before going 0-18 in the Big East."<ref name=miller20170928/> Other basketball media members called the schedule "embarrassing,"<ref name=miller20170928/><ref name=hladik20170912>[https://thespun.com/big-east/georgetown/georgetown-basketballs-non-conference-schedule-is-ridiculously-weak Hladik, Matt, "Georgetown Basketball's Non-Conference Schedule Is Ridiculously Weak," thespuncom, September 12, 2017, 5:39 p.m. Retrieved July 27, 2018]</ref> "pathetic,"<ref name=cavallaro20171228>[https://bustingbrackets.com/2017/12/28/georgetown-basketball-weak-schedule-hurts-hoyas/ Cavallaro, Brad, "Georgetown Basketball: Weak schedule hurts the Hoyas," bustingbrackets.com, December 28, 2017. Retrieved July 28, 2018.]</ref> "ridiculously weak,"<ref name=hladik20170912/> "atrocious,"<ref>[https://collegebasketball.nbcsports.com/2017/09/12/georgetowns-non-conference-schedule-is-terrible/ Dauster, Rob, "Georgetown's non-conference schedule is terrible," nbcsports.com,  September 12, 2017, 1:50 PM EDT, Retrieved July 28, 2018]</ref> "among the worst non-conference schedule I have ever seen,"<ref name=hladik20170912/> "perhaps the worst non-con[ference] schedule ever,"<ref name=hladik20170912/> and "the worst non-conference basketball schedule ever."<ref name=steinberg20170912/> Critics also noted that even if the Hoyas had an unexpectedly strong showing in Big East play, the non-conference schedule's weakness would work against Georgetown when the selection committee for the  2018 NCAA Tournament made its picks the following March,<ref name=hladik20170912/> virtually precluding Georgetown's consideration for the NCAA Tournament and even for the [[2018 National Invitation Tournament]].<ref name=cavallaro20171228/> Ewing made no apologies for how he scheduled the team, dismissing concerns about the non-conference schedule by saying, "It's all a work in progress. To me everything is a work in progress to get ready for the Big East. The Big East is where everything starts for me. The Big East is a make or break for us...My guys are coming off two poor years, and it is my job to mend their egos and to get them to believe in themselves again. The Big East is what it's all about. Get our guys believing in themselves and get ready for the Big East competition."<ref name=247sports20180308>[https://247sports.com/college/georgetown/Article/Revisiting-Georgetowns-2017-2018-Non-Conference-Schedule-115990161/ Anonymous, "Revisiting Georgetown's 2017-2018 Non-Conference Schedule," 247sports.com, March 8, 2018, 3:43 PM. Retrieved July 28, 2018.]</ref>

Regardless of the debate over their schedule, the Hoyas began their season two months to the day after it was announced, on November 12, opening a three-game homestand by facing Jacksonville at [[Capital One Arena]], as the Verizon Center had been renamed in August 2017.<ref>[https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2017/aug/9/verizon-center-renamed-capital-one-arena/ Paras, Matthew, "Verizon Center renamed Capital One Arena," washingtontimes.com, August 9, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> It was Ewing's first game as a head coach at any level, and in honor of the occasion Ewing's former college and NBA rival [[Michael Jordan]], former Georgetown and NBA players [[Alonzo Mourning]] and [[Dikembe Mutombo]], [[Washington Wizards]] and former Georgetown player [[Otto Porter|Otto Porter Jr.]], Wizards head coach [[Scott Brooks]], and Ewing's former New York Knicks coach and television analyst [[Jeff Van Gundy]] all were in the crowd,<ref name=ap20171112>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988416 Anonymous, "Patrick Ewing gets first win as Hoyas defeat Jacksonville," Associated Press, November 12, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref><ref name=wallace20171112>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/nba-stars-align-for-patrick-ewing-as-new-georgetown-coach-gets-a-win-in-debut/2017/11/12/611887ae-c7ea-11e7-b0cf-7689a9f2d84e_story.html Wallace, Ava, "NBA stars align for Patrick Ewing as new Georgetown coach gets a win in debut," washingtonpost.com, November 12, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> and Ewing told the press that his high-school coach also was at the game.<ref name=wallace20171112/> The crowd cheered loudly when Ewing first walked onto the court about 10 minutes before the opening tipoff,<ref name=ap20171112/> and gave him an ovation when the spotlight fell on him during pregame introductions.<ref name=ap20171112/> The Hoyas held the Dolphins – who were coming off [[2016–17 Jacksonville Dolphins men's basketball team|their first winning season]] in six years<ref name=wallace20171118>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/georgetown-basketball-is-3-0-but-the-wins-mean-less-than-the-experience/2017/11/18/de4faab0-cca2-11e7-8321-481fd63f174d_story.html Wallace, Ava, "Georgetown basketball is 3-0, but the wins mean less than the experience," washingtonpost.com, November 18, 2017 Retrieved August 14, 2018]</ref> – to 23.3 percent shooting from the field in the first half<ref name=ap20171112/> and 32.7 percent for the game<ref name=ap20171112/> as Georgetown cruised to a 73–57 victory<ref name=ap20171112/> and Ewing's first head-coaching win. Jesse Govan led the Hoyas with a [[double-double]] (20 points and 15 rebounds),<ref name=ap20171112/> and Marcus Derrickson also scored 20.<ref name=ap20171112/>

Over the next six days, the homestand continued with victories over Mount St. Mary's, which had not defeated Georgetown since [[1960–61 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1961]],<ref name=wallace20171118/> and Maryland Eastern Shore, which was missing five players projected preseason as starters because of eligibility problems and other reasons.<ref name=wallace20171118/> Against Mount St. Mary's, the Hoyas scored 102 points<ref name=ap20171115>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988424 Anonymous, "Govan leads Georgetown to another victory, 102-68," Associated Press, November 15, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> – their first 100-plus-point game since they scored 105 against [[2016–17 USC Upstate Spartans men's basketball team|South Carolina Upstate]] in their season opener the previous year<ref name=ap20171115/> – and Jesse Govan had his second straight double-double with 20 points and 14 rebounds,<ref name=ap20171115/> while Jahvon Blair contributed 19 points and five assists,<ref name=ap20171115/> Jagan Moseley scored 15 points and also recorded five assists,<ref name=ap20171115/> and Kaleb Johnson and Jamorko Pickett each had 14 points and seven rebounds.<ref name=ap20171115/> Three days later against Maryland Eastern Shore, Johnson scored a career-high 24 points,<ref name=ap20171118>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988486 Anonymous, "Govan, Derrickson double-doubles lift Georgetown past UMES," Associated Press, November 18, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> Govan had his third straight double-double (23 points and 14 rebounds),<ref name=ap20171118/> Marcus Derrickson had his third career double-double (14 points and 10 rebounds),<ref name=ap20171118/> Blair scored 12 points,<ref>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400988486 Maryland Eastern Shore vs. Georgetown – Box Score – November 18, 2017 – ESPN]</ref> and Jonathan Mulmore posted 10 points and recorded five assists.<ref name=ap20171118/>

Beginning the season with a record of 3–0 for the first time since [[2014–15 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2014–2015]], the Hoyas traveled to [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond]], [[Virginia]], to meet Richmond at the [[Robins Center]] a week later<ref name=ap20171125>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988498 Anonymous, "Georgetown holds on for 82-76 win over Richmond," Associated Press, November 25, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> in Georgetown's only non-conference game of the season away from Capital One Arena; it was part of a home-and-home series in which Richmond would visit Georgetown [[2018–19 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the following season]]. Richmond, although only 1–3 on the season entering the game,<ref name=wallace20171125>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/georgetown-stays-unbeaten-under-patrick-ewing-with-road-victory-over-richmond/2017/11/25/cb7c6930-d221-11e7-9d3a-bcbe2af58c3a_story.html Wallace, Eva, "Georgetown stays unbeaten under Patrick Ewing with victory at Richmond," washingtonpost.com, November 25, 2017 Retrieved August 14, 2018]</ref> had been a [[2017 National Invitation Tournament]] quarterfinalist<ref name=wallace20170912/> and as Georgetown's second-strongest non-conference opponent<ref name=miller20170928/> posed the biggest challenge thus far in Georgetown's young season. With former Georgetown head coach [[John Thompson (basketball)|John Thompson Jr.]] making the trip and looking on from the stands,<ref name=wallace20171125/> the Hoyas led by only 40–39 at halftime<ref name=ap20171125/> and had to fend off a Richmond surge in which the Spiders took a 59–57 lead with 9:26 left to play<ref name=ap20171125/> before pulling back ahead and hanging on for an 82–76 win.<ref name=ap20171125/> In a balanced Georgetown attack, Marcus Derrickson scored 16 points and grabbed nine rebounds,<ref name=ap20171125/> Jonathan Mulmore added 15 points and eight assists,<ref name=ap20171125/> Jessie Govan had 14 points and six rebounds,<ref name=ap20171125/> Jamorko Pickett scored 12 points and pulled down seven rebounds,<ref name=ap20171125/> and Kaleb Johnson added 11 points.<ref name=ap20171125/> The win gave Georgetown its first 4–0 start since the 2014–2015 season.

By the time the Hoyas returned to Capital One Arena on November 28 to begin an eight-game homestand by meeting Maine, their first five opponents had a combined record of 9–25 (.265) on the season, and two of them had won only one game.<ref name=wang20171127/> Georgetown defeated Maine – a  team that was missing three of its starters and had a record of 1–6 entering the game<ref name=wang20171127/> – but the Hoyas′ strength of schedule fell to 348th or 349th, depending on the ranking system, out of 351 Division I teams.<ref name=wang20171127/> Georgetown followed up over the next 11 days with wins over Coppin State, Howard, and North Carolina A&T. Georgetown cruised to easy wins in all four games, and the resulting 5–0, 6–0, 7–0, and 8–0 records for the Hoyas represented their first start with each of those records since [[2010–11 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the 2010–2011 season]]. The Coppin State game was the Hoyas′ fourth consecutive and fourth overall appearance in the annual [[BB&T Classic]], and they improved their all-time record in the Classic to 4–0, but by the time they had beaten Howard, their strength of schedule had fallen to 351st, the weakest among NCAA Division I teams.<ref>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/georgetown-makes-way-through-cupcake-line-eases-past-howard/2017/12/07/02823d96-db7e-11e7-b1a8-62589434a581_story.html Wallace, Ava, "Georgetown makes way through cupcake line, eases past Howard," washingtonpost.com, December 7, 2017 Retrieved August 14, 2018]</ref> Jessie Govan scored 16 points and grabbed eight rebounds against Maine,<ref name=ap20171128>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988501 Anonymous, "Johnson's 18 helps Hoyas beat Maine 76-55, remain unbeaten," Associated Press, November 28, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> then recorded three straight double-doubles – his fourth, fifth, and sixth of the season – with a season-high 26 points and a career-high 16 rebounds against Coppin State,<ref name=ap20171203>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988511 Anonymous, "Georgetown stays perfect with 76-60 win over Coppin St.," Associated Press, December 3, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> 24 points against Howard in a game in which he tied his career best with 16 rebounds and also blocked three shots,<ref name=ap20171207>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988518 Anonymous, "Govan has 24 points, 16 boards as Georgetown beats Howard," Associated Press, December 7, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> and 22 points and 15 rebounds against North Carolina A&T.<ref name=ap20171209>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988520 Anonymous, "Georgetown stays perfect with 83-74 win over NC A&T," Associated Press, December 9, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> Kaleb Johnson scored 18 against both Maine<ref name=ap20171128/> and Howard<ref name=ap20171207/> – in the Howard game on 6-for-6 shooting from the field, including 2-for-2 from three-point range, and a 4-for-4 performance from the free-throw line<ref name=ap20171207/> – and he finished with 10 points against North Carolina A&T.<ref name=ap20171209/> Marcus Derrickson scored 12 points and went 6–for–6 in free throws against Maine<ref name=ap20171128/> and had 13 points against Coppin State,<ref name=ap20171203/> and he contributed 16 points and nine rebounds against Howard.<ref name=ap20171207/> Jamorko Pickett finished with 13 points against Coppin State<ref name=ap20171203/> and 12 against North Carolina A&T.<ref name=ap20171209/> In the Maine game, Jonathan Mulmore scored 10 points and recorded five assists,<ref name=ap20171209/> while Jahvon Blair came off the bench to add 11 points.<ref name=ap20171209/>

North Carolina A&T's loss to Georgetown dropped the Aggies to 5–4, but they were the only team with a winning record the Hoyas had faced all season.<ref name=wang20171209/> Defeating North Carolina A&T gave Georgetown an 8–0 record<ref name=svrluga20171215>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/hoyas-schedule-is-a-fine-way-to-build-confidence-and-a-lousy-way-to-make-anyone-care/2017/12/14/1ff4732c-e109-11e7-bbd0-9dfb2e37492a_story.html Svrluga, Barry, "Hoyas’ schedule is a fine way to build confidence and a lousy way to make anyone care," washingtonpost.com, December 15, 2017. Retrieved July 27, 2018]</ref> and made the Hoyas one of only six [[NCAA Division I]] teams without a loss during the season.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> However, Georgetown also had the weakest [[strength of schedule]] – 351st out of 351 – among Division I schools.<ref name=wang20171209/><ref name=svrluga20171215/> By the time the Hoyas beat North Carolina A&T on December 9, Georgetown's previous seven opponents were a combined 13-54 (.194) on the season,<ref name=wang20171209/> and the Hoyas′ previous three opponents (Maine, Coppin State, and Howard) had a combined record of 2–26 (.071).<ref name=wang20171209/> By December 15 – the eve of the Hoyas′ meeting with Syracuse – Georgetown's first eight opponents were a combined 24-64 (.273) on the season.<ref name=svrluga20171215/><ref name=ap20171216>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400986140 Anonymous, "Syracuse comebacks to beat Georgetown 86-79 in OT," Associated Press, December 16, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> The lackluster games resulted in lackluster attendance: The crowd of 9,212 for the season opener against Jacksonville left the 20,356-seat Capital One Arena less than half-full, and since then the Hoyas had averaged 5,247 fans per game<ref name=svrluga20171215/> and never had reached 6,500 for any game.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> When reporters again asked Ewing immediately after the North Carolina A&T game about the unambitious schedule he had put together, he dismissed their concerns by saying, "It's a great schedule, a great schedule. All the people worried about the schedule are all you guys."<ref name=wang20171209/>

The Hoyas had a week off before facing Syracuse, Georgetown's archrival in the original Big East, and during that week the letter "S" was "prohibited" on the Georgetown campus, being covered over or X-ed out everywhere it appeared on a sign.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> The game was Georgetown's only real challenge of the nonconference schedule, and it pitted Patrick Ewing against [[Jim Boeheim]] – Syracuse's head coach back in Ewing's playing days at Georgetown – as head coaches for the first time,<ref name=ap20171216/> prompting nostalgia about the early 1980s heyday of the original Big East Conference. Neither team led by more than five points during the first half,<ref name=ap20171216/> and the Hoyas held a 28–24 lead at halftime.<ref name=ap20171216/> Georgetown pulled out to a 53–40 lead in the second half<ref name=ap20171216/> before the Orange, led by freshman [[small forward]] [[Oshae Brissett]] – who scored only one point in the first half but 24 after halftime – began a comeback, going on a 5–0 scoring run to close the gap to 53–45 with 9:55 remaining in regulation.<ref name=ap20171216/> Georgetown still led 64–57 when Marcus Derrickson fouled out with 5:23 left in the second half.<ref name=ap20171216/> With a minute left in regulation, Syracuse sophomore guard Frank Howard stripped the ball from Jesse Govan and scored on a layup to tie the game 69–69, but then Syracuse missed three straight shots and the game remained tied at 69–69 at the end of regulation.<ref name=ap20171216/> Syracuse sophomore guard [[Tyus Battle]] led the Orange in overtime, scoring eight points after the end of regulation,<ref name=ap20171216/> including a three-pointer that put Syracuse ahead for good at 72–69.<ref name=ap20171216/> Syracuse, which had outscored Georgetown 29–15 after Derrickson fouled out,<ref name=ap20171216/> won 86–79, dealing the Hoyas their first loss of the season. The win snapped a two-game Orange losing streak against the Hoyas<ref name=ap20171216/> and was their first road win against Georgetown since [[2010–11 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2011]],<ref name=ap20171216/> while the Hoyas missed both their first chance to beat Syracuse three games in a row since a four-win streak between [[1999–2000 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2000]] and [[2001–02 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2002]]<ref name=ap20171216/> and their only chance to pick up a quality win during their non-conference schedule.<ref name=ap20171216/> Both teams shot 10-for-27 (37 percent) from the field<ref name=ap20171216/> and both had 16 turnovers.<ref name=ap20171216/> Jessie Govan had 21 points and eight rebounds<ref name=ap20171216/> and logged a career-high 42 minutes,<ref name=wang20171220>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/georgetown-bounces-back-from-syracuse-loss-by-running-away-from-north-texas/2017/12/20/109e0800-e5b6-11e7-ab50-621fe0588340_story.html Wang, Gene, "Georgetown bounces back from Syracuse loss by running away from North Texas," washingtonpost.com, December 20, 2017 Retrieved August 14, 2018]</ref> Jagan Mosely came off the bench to add 20 points,<ref name=ap20171216/> Marcus Derrickson had 14 points and eight rebounds,<ref name=ap20171216/> and Jamorko Pickett scored 12 points.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400986140 Syracuse vs. Georgetown – Box Score – December 16, 2017 – ESPN]</ref>

On December 19, Georgetown announced that freshman center Chris Sodom had been dismissed from the team for violating team rules;<ref name=bonesteel20171219>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/sports/wp/2017/12/19/georgetown-basketball-dismisses-freshman-center-over-violation-of-team-rules/ Bonesteel, Matt, "Georgetown basketball dismisses freshman center over violation of team rules," washingtonpost.com, December 19, 2017 Retrieved August 12 2018]</ref> it later was revealed that his dismissal stemmed from his involvement in an off-campus altercation.<ref>[https://www.casualhoya.com/2018/10/11/17965450/antwan-walker-dismissed-from-program Anonymous, "Antwan Walker Dismissed from Program," casualhoya.com, October 11, 2018, 4:15 p.m. EDT Retrieved March 31, 2019]</ref> Sodom had had little impact on the team, appearing in only six games and playing only 27 minutes as a Hoya,<ref name=bonesteel20171219/> but his departure left Georgetown with a shortage of depth among its "big men;"<ref name=bonesteel20171219/> with Sodom off the team, Ewing's only option for the rest of the season as a backup for center Jesse Govan and forward Marcus Derrickson became freshman forward Antwan Walker.<ref name=bonesteel20171219/><ref name=wallace20180524>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/sports/wp/2018/04/11/georgetowns-jessie-govan-will-test-the-nba-draft-waters/ Wallace, Ava, "Georgetown center Jessie Govan withdraws from the NBA draft, will return for senior season," washingtonpost.com, May 24, 2018 Retrieved August 12, 2018]</ref><ref name=wallace20171223>[https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/colleges/georgetown-wraps-up-weak-nonconference-slate-with-rout-of-alabama-aandm/2017/12/23/edb30178-e769-11e7-833f-155031558ff4_story.html Wallace, Ava, "Georgetown wraps up weak nonconference slate with rout of Alabama A&M," washingtonpost.com, December 23, 2017 Retrieved August 14, 2018]</ref>

The Hoyas completed their non-conference schedule with two more home games, beating North Texas in the first meeting between the schools<ref name=ap20171220>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988536 Anonymous, "Derrickson, Govan lead Georgetown past North Texas 75-63," Associated Press, December 20, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref>  and then defeating winless Alabama A&M.<ref name=ap20171223>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988545 Anonymous, "Walker scores 16 in first start, leads Hoyas in 89-49 win," Associated Press, December 23, 2017. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> Against North Texas, with Ewing's former New York Knicks teammate [[John Starks (basketball)|John Starks]] looking on from the stands,<ref name=wang20171220/> Marcus Derrickson led the Hoyas with 17 points<ref name=ap20171220/> and Jessie Govan had his ninth career double-double and seventh double-double of the season with 12 points and 14 rebounds,<ref name=ap20171220/> while Jonathan Mulmore finished with 12 points and six assists.<ref name=ap20171220/> Three days later in the rout of Alabama A&M – which entered the game with a record of 0–12 and ranked 344th in RPI among the 351 Division I schools<ref name=wallace20171223/> – Antwan Walker made his first collegiate start and first appearance in a game since December 9,<ref name=wallace20171223/> played a career-high 15 minutes<ref name=wallace20171223/> and scored in double figures for the first time with 16 points on 6-of-7 shooting from the field and 4-for-4 from the free-throw line,<ref name=ap20171223/> while Jahvon Blair, making his second collegiate start, scored 13 points.<ref name=ap20171223/> Against Alabama A&M, Jessie Govan had another double-double (11 points and 11 rebounds), his eighth of the season<ref name=ap20171223/> and the tenth of his career, while Jamorko Pickett and Kaleb Johnson added 10 points each.<ref name=ap20171223/>

The Hoyas completed their non-conference schedule with a 10–1 record, their best start to a season since they opened 10–1 in [[2012–13 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|2012–2013]]. However, their strength of schedule was 350th among the 351 teams after they defeated North Texas<ref>[https://herosports.com/college-basketball/georgetown-basketball-schedule-patrick-ewing-ahah Doughty, Andrew "Georgetown's Non-Conference Schedule is a Joke," herosports.com, December 22, 2018, 11:45 a.m. EST. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> and fell to 351st and last after they beat Alabama A&M.<ref name=zielonka20180308>[https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2018/mar/8/patrick-ewing-end-first-season-coaching-georgetown/ Zielonka, Adam, "At end of first season coaching Georgetown, Ewing not ready to reflect," washingtontimes.com, March 8, 2018. Retrieved July 29, 2018]</ref> Sports pundits understood Ewing's desire to pad the team's schedule given its limited prospects for the season and its need to rebuild in terms of both talent and confidence.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> However, sports commentators also viewed the nonconference portion of Georgetown's schedule as harming the team's chances of making the NCAA Tournament even if it won most of its conference games,<ref name=svrluga20171215/> as well as poorly preparing the Hoyas for the rigors of the upcoming Big East season.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> They also saw it as a missed opportunity to market Georgetown's otherwise faded national brand by highlighting Ewing's return to the school via nationally noted nonconference games, such as those that might have occurred if Georgetown had not withdrawn from the November PK80-Phil Knight Tournament.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> On the eve of the Syracuse game, college basketball analyst [[Ken Pomeroy]] opined that the Hoyas would have to go an unexpected 12–6 in the upcoming Big East season to ensure an NCAA Tournament bid and that even an equally unexpected record of 11–7 might make it difficult for the selection committee to justify a bid.<ref name=svrluga20171215/> Asked by reporters after the Alabama A&M game whether he felt his team was prepared for Big East play, Ewing was noncommittal, saying, "That's yet to be determined. We just have to stay focused and continue to work hard. Even though we're, what, 10-1 right now, we can't be happy with that. We have to stay hungry. No one expects us to be successful, and we have to have a chip on our shoulder about that. We have to continue to grind. At the end of the year, we'll see where we lie."<ref name=wallace20171223/>

===Conference schedule===

Georgetown completed its eight-game homestand and opened its Big East season on December 27 with a 91–89 double-overtime loss to [[2017–18 Butler Bulldogs men's basketball team|Butler]], despite pulling out to a 20-point lead in the first half and holding a 42-24 lead over the Bulldogs at halftime;<ref name=ap20171227>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988547 Anonymous, "Butler rallies to 91-89 2OT win over Georgetown," Associated Press, December 27, 2017. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> Marcus Derrickson (23 points and 11 rebounds)<ref name=ap20171227/> and Jesse Govan (19 points and 13 rebounds)<ref name=ap20171227/> both had double-doubles, and Jahvon Blair went 11-for-12 from the free-throw line and scored 17 points.<ref name=ap20171227/> The Hoyas then embarked on a two-game road trip in which they finished 2017 with a loss at [[2017–18 Marquette Golden Eagles men's basketball team|Marquette]] and began 2018 with their first conference victory of the season in a game at [[2017–18 DePaul Blue Demons men's basketball team|DePaul]]. Derrickson scored 20 points at Marquette,<ref name=boxscore20171230>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400988554 Georgetown vs. Marquette – Box Score – December 30, 2017 – ESPN Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> and 24 at DePaul,<ref name=ap20180102>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988558 Anonymous, "Govan has 25 points, 12 boards as Georgetown beats DePaul," Associated Press, January 2, 2018. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> while Kaleb Johnson finished with 12 points at Marquette<ref name=boxscore20171230/> and Jahvon Blair had a 15-point game against DePaul.<ref name=ap20180102/> Govan had double-doubles in both games, with 11 points and 12 rebounds at Marquette<ref name=boxscore20171230/> and 25 points and 12 boards at DePaul.<ref name=ap20180102/>

Georgetown returned to Capital One Arena for a one-sided loss to [[2017–18 Creighton Bluejays men's basketball team|Creighton]] in which the Hoyas trailed from the opening basket and the Bluejays led by double figures from halfway through the first half through the end of the game;<ref name=ap20180106>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988561 Anonymous, "Hegner leads Creighton's 3-point parade in 90-66 victory," Associated Press, January 6, 2018. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref><ref name=playbyplay20180106>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/playbyplay?gameId=400988561 Georgetown vs. Marquette – Play-by-Play – January 6, 2018 – ESPN Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> with 11 points, Jahvon Blair was the only Hoya to score in double figures,<ref name=ap20180106/><ref name=boxscore20180106>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400988554 Georgetown vs. Marquette – Box Score – January 6, 2018 – ESPN Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> while Kaleb Johnson grabbed 10 rebounds.<ref name=boxscore20180106/> Three days later, Georgetown visited [[Madison Square Garden]] and defeated [[2017–18 St. John's Red Storm men's basketball team|St. John's]] to improve to 2–3 in conference play; Govan had another double-double, scoring 18 points and pulling down 13 rebounds,<ref name=ap20180110>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988561 Anonymous, "Georgetown's Ewing tops St. John's Mullin 1 more time at MSG," Associated Press, January 10, 2018. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> Derrickson added 17 points,<ref name=ap20180110/> and Jagan Moseley contributed 13.<ref>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400988566 Georgetown vs. St. John's – Box Score – January 9, 2018 – ESPN Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> With former St. John's head coach [[Lou Carnesecca]] in the stands,<ref name=ap20180110/> the two teams played a lackluster game that betrayed how far the two programs had fallen since their mid-1980s heyday in the original Big East Conference when Carnesecca coached the Red Storm, Ewing played for Georgetown, St. John's head coach [[Chris Mullin (basketball)|Chris Mullin]] played for St. John's, and the two teams were national powers and faced off in nationally prominent games.<ref name=ap20180110/> However, the meeting was the first between Ewing and Mullin as head coaches,<ref name=ap20180110/> and the game also marked the return of Ewing to Madison Square Garden, where he had played with the New York Knicks in the NBA, and it prompted much nostalgia about both the old Big East and Ewing's 15-year Knicks career;<ref name=ap20180110/> the crowd cheered heartily for Ewing from the moment he came out onto the court and chanted "Patrick! Patrick!" as he exited after the conclusion of the game.<ref name=ap20180110/>

In their next game, the Hoyas faced a ranked opponent for the first time in the season when they traveled to meet No. 13 [[2017–18 Seton Hall Pirates men's basketball team|Seton Hall]] at the [[Prudential Center]] in [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]], [[New Jersey]], on January 13,<ref name=ap20180113>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988572 Anonymous, "No. 13 Seton Hall beats Georgetown," Associated Press, January 13, 2018. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> the first time they had gone without a ranked opponent until mid-January since [[2003–04 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|the 2003-2004 season]]. Undefeated at home for the season at 10–0,<ref name=ap20180113/> the Pirates were celebrating the 25th anniversary of [[1992–93 Seton Hall Pirates men's basketball team|the 1992–1993 Pirates team]] that won both the Big East regular season championship and the [[1993 Big East men's basketball tournament|1993 Big East tournament]],<ref name=ap20180113/> and that season's head coach, [[P. J. Carlesimo]],<ref name=ap20180113/> and [[Artūras Karnišovas]], [[General manager (basketball)|general manager]] of the [[Denver Nuggets]] and a member of the 1992–1993 Seton Hall team, were in the audience.<ref name=ap20180113/> The Hoyas staked themselves to a 12–3 lead to start the game,<ref name=ap20180113/> but the Pirates took advantage of Georgetown turnovers to come back with a 29–10 scoring run in the final 11 minutes of the first half<ref name=ap20180113/> and go into the locker room with a 44–31 at halftime.<ref name=ap20180113/> In the second half, the Pirates pulled out to a 16–point advantage<ref name=ap20180113/> before the Hoyas cut Seton Hall's lead to 60–52 with eight minutes to play,<ref name=ap20180113/> but Seton Hall extended its lead to 62–52 with 6:29 left<ref name=ap20180113/> and to 69-54 with 3:28 remaining<ref name=ap20180113/> on the way to a 74–61 win.<ref name=ap20180113/> It was Seton Hall's fifth straight victory over Georgetown,<ref name=ap20180113/> and the Pirates improved their all-time record against the Hoyas to 47–57<ref name=ap20180113/> – dating back to the first meeting between the schools on [[1909–10 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|December 10, 1909]]<ref name=ap20180113/> – and to 21–41 since the two teams joined the original Big East Conference as charter members in [[1979–80 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1979]].<ref name=ap20180113/> Marcus Derrickson led the Hoyas with 18 points,<ref name=ap20180113/> while Kaleb Johnson scored 14 points<ref>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/boxscore?gameId=400988572 Georgetown vs. St. John's – Box Score – January 13, 2018 – ESPN Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> and Jahvon Blair and Jesse Govan had 11 each.<ref name=ap20180113/>

Four days later, the Hoyas were at Capital One Arena to open a three-game homestand by playing another ranked opponent, No. 1 [[2017–18 Villanova Wildcats men's basketball team|Villanova]].<ref name=fendrich20180117>[https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/recap?gameId=400988577 Fendrich, Howard, "No. 1 Villanova leads by 44, beats Ewing, Georgetown 88-56," Associated Press, January 17, 2018. Retrieved August 6, 2018]</ref> It was the first time Ewing had faced Villanova in any capacity since the Wildcats upset the Hoyas in his final game as a college player to win the national championship in the [[1985 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament|1985 NCAA tournament]].<ref name=fendrich20180117/> The game quickly became a blowout, as Villanova went on an 18–0 scoring run to take a 31–8 lead in the first half.<ref name=fendrich20180117/> By halftime, when Villanova led 42–20,<ref name=fendrich20180117/> Georgetown had more turnovers (nine) than baskets (eight),<ref name=fendrich20180117/> and had shot only 8-for-26 (30.8 percent) from the field,<ref name=fendrich20180117/> including 0-for-8 in three-pointers.<ref name=fendrich20180117/> During the second half, Villanova continued to extend its lead, which reached its peak at 88–44 with about {{frac|3|1|2}} minutes remaining. With about {{frac|2|1|2}} minutes left, Villanova head coach [[Jay Wright (basketball)|Jay Wright]] took his starters out of the game, and with the Wildcats′ bench players on the floor, the Hoyas concluded the game with a 12–0 scoring run,<ref name=fendrich20180117/> closing to 88–56 at the final buzzer.<ref name=fendrich20180117/> For the game, the Wildcats shot 17-for-33 (51.5 percent) from three-point range, while the Hoyas shot only 4-for-15 (26.7 percent) from the beyond the arc.<ref name=fendrich20180117/> Jesse Govan, the only Georgetown player to score in double figures, finished with 12 points,<ref name=fendrich20180117/> and Trey Dickerson left the game with [[back spasm]]s during the first half.<ref name=fendrich20180117/> It was Villanova's seventh straight victory over Georgetown, the Wildcats′ longest winning streak against the Hoyas since the schools first met in [[1921–22 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|1922]].<ref name=fendrich20180117/> The 32-point loss was Georgetown's worst since [[1974–75 Georgetown Hoyas men's basketball team|December 10, 1974]], when [[1974–75 Maryland Terrapins men's basketball team|Maryland]] beat the Hoyas by 33 points, 104–71,<ref name=fendrich20180117/> and it dropped the Hoyas to 12–6 on the season, 2–5 in the Big East. Georgetown's easy non-conference schedule had inflated the Hoyas′ overall record<ref name=fendrich20180117/> and, when the press asked him what the game said about the true contrast between the state of the Georgetown's men's basketball program and that of a national power like Villanova, Ewing replied, "I'm not even thinking about that. All I'm thinking about is that they're a good team and tonight was their night. That's it. . .I've had my butt kicked before – fortunately it was as a player – and all I can do is get ready for the next one. You can't dwell on it. Just got to look at the film and make adjustments and get ready for the next game."<ref name=fendrich20180117/>
